track.name: ai-nocode
track.label: AI Automation with No-Code
track.summary: Build powerful AI-driven automations without writing code. Master Zapier, Make.com, and n8n to connect your business tools and run AI steps inside your workflows.

phases.title: Automation Fundamentals
phases.description: Understand what automation is, how triggers and actions work, and how to identify the best candidates for automation in your daily work.

phases.title: Zapier & Make.com
phases.description: Build multi-step zaps and Make scenarios with filters, formatters, error handling, and webhook-based triggers.

phases.title: n8n Basics
phases.description: Explore the open-source n8n platform, deploy self-hosted flows, and configure integrations with common business tools.

phases.title: AI Steps in Automations
phases.description: Add OpenAI and Claude actions inside Zapier and Make scenarios to summarise, classify, extract, and generate content automatically.

phases.title: Connecting Business Tools
phases.description: Integrate Slack, Gmail, Notion, Airtable, and Google Sheets into your automations to keep teams and data in sync.

phases.title: Building Real Workflows
phases.description: Design and ship end-to-end automation projects from requirements through testing, error monitoring, and maintenance.

topics.title: Triggers, Actions, and Conditions
topics.description: Learn the building blocks of every automation: what fires a workflow, what it does, and how conditions filter which runs proceed.

steps.d: Write down what fires your automation (trigger), what it does (action), and what must be true for it to run (condition) for one daily task.
Draw a box labeled 'Trigger', connect it to 'Action 1', then 'Action 2' and label what happens at each step.
Follow how data moves through your workflow: what information is passed from trigger to action, and where a field mapping might be needed.
Modify your diagram to add 'Only run if [condition]' (e.g. only if email has attachment, only if amount exceeds $100).
Describe your trigger-condition-action workflow to a colleague in 2-3 sentences and confirm they understand when it will run.

topics.title: When to Automate: Finding Good Candidates
topics.description: Apply a simple decision framework to identify repetitive, rule-based tasks in your work that are high-value automation targets.

steps.d: Write down 10-15 tasks you do by hand or in separate tools each week (e.g. forwarding emails, logging data, sending reminders).
For each task, estimate minutes per occurrence and weekly frequency, multiply to find total weekly time spent.
Highlight the tasks that take the most total time or happen most frequently, excluding any requiring judgment or customisation.
For each high-value task, ask: 'Is it repetitive? Is it rule-based? Can I describe the rule clearly?' and mark those answering yes to all three.
Order your best automation candidates by time saved and setup difficulty, then pick the easiest one to build first.

topics.title: No-Code Automation Tools Overview
topics.description: Compare Zapier, Make.com, n8n, and similar platforms on capability, cost, and complexity so you can pick the right tool for each job.

steps.d: Look up current pricing for Zapier, Make.com, and n8n for 1000 tasks per month and note data-storage limits.
Sign up for a free trial of Zapier and Make.com, connect two simple apps to each, and time how long setup takes.
Spend 10 minutes on the n8n GitHub community and Zapier Academy to evaluate which platform feels better documented for your skill level.
List the 5-10 apps you use daily and check whether Zapier, Make, and n8n support them in their app libraries.
Based on cost, integrations, ease of use, and support, pick one platform to learn and write one sentence explaining your choice.

topics.title: Building Your First Zap
topics.description: Set up a two-step Zap from scratch, connect two apps, map data fields, and test the run end-to-end.

steps.d: Sign up for Zapier, verify your email, and connect at least one app you use daily such as Gmail, Google Sheets, or Slack.
Pick a trigger like 'New email matching search' or 'New spreadsheet row' and configure it to find the data you want.
Connect a second app as the action step (e.g. save email to folder, append data to spreadsheet) and map the relevant fields.
Click 'Test' to send sample data through the automation and verify the action runs correctly without errors.
Turn on the Zap and trigger it manually with real data (e.g. send a test email) to confirm end-to-end operation.

topics.title: Multi-Step Zaps and Filters
topics.description: Chain multiple actions in a single workflow, apply filter steps to stop runs that don't meet conditions, and use Paths for branching logic.

steps.d: Open a working Zap and insert a new action after the first one (e.g. if saving emails to a folder, add logging data to a spreadsheet).
Add a filter between your trigger and first action that restricts runs to certain data (e.g. 'only if subject contains urgent').
Add a Path that branches your workflow: 'If [condition], do this; else, do that' (e.g. if amount > $1000, notify manager).
Run sample data through both the true and false branches of your Path and verify each branch executes correctly.
Insert another action after your Paths to consolidate results or send a final notification, then test the complete workflow.

topics.title: Error Handling and Webhooks
topics.description: Configure error notifications and retries in Zapier, and use webhook triggers to receive data from any service with an HTTP endpoint.

steps.d: In Zapier settings, enable error notifications via email or Slack to alert you when a Zap fails or task limit is reached.
Temporarily misconfigure a field mapping in a Zap and run the trigger to see what the error notification looks like.
Create a new Zap with a Webhook trigger, copy the Zapier webhook URL, and test sending an HTTP POST request to it.
Find your Zap's error handling settings and set it to 'Retry failed tasks' with a delay between attempts.
Modify a Zap to add an error-handler path that logs failed runs to a Slack channel or spreadsheet for review.

topics.title: Introduction to n8n
topics.description: Understand n8n's node-based interface, install a local or cloud instance, and build your first basic workflow.

steps.d: Either install n8n on your machine with Docker or sign up for n8n Cloud, then log in and create a blank workflow.
Search for a trigger node (e.g. 'Webhook' or 'Schedule'), drag it into the canvas, and configure it to fire on your chosen trigger.
Add a second node such as HTTP Request or Slack and connect it to your trigger by drawing a line between them.
Fill in the action's fields (URL, credentials, data format) and click 'Test' to verify data flows from trigger to action.
Click 'Execute' to run the entire workflow and check the output in n8n's debug panel to confirm success.

topics.title: Building Self-Hosted Flows
topics.description: Run n8n on your own infrastructure, connect credentials securely, and manage workflow versions with n8n's built-in tools.

steps.d: Follow the n8n self-hosting guide to deploy n8n to a machine you control (AWS, DigitalOcean, or your own hardware), then log in.
Add API keys and passwords for your business apps to n8n's Credentials section without storing them in plaintext.
Create a workflow with 3-5 nodes that reads from one app, transforms data, and writes to another app using your stored credentials.
Add a Schedule trigger to your workflow and set it to run on a specific day and time (e.g. daily at 9 AM, every Monday).
Let the workflow run for a full week and check the execution history to verify it ran on schedule without errors.

topics.title: Common n8n Integrations
topics.description: Configure the most frequently used n8n nodes: HTTP Request, Webhook, Gmail, Slack, Google Sheets, and Notion.

steps.d: In a new n8n workflow, add a Gmail node as a trigger to watch for new emails matching a label or filter.
Add a Google Sheets node as the next step to append received email data (subject, sender, date) to a spreadsheet.
Add a Slack node that sends a message to a channel with the email subject whenever a new message arrives.
Add a Notion node to create a database page for each important email, pulling in the subject, sender, and link.
Send yourself a test email and verify data appears in Sheets, a Slack message is sent, and a Notion page is created.

topics.title: OpenAI Actions in Zapier
topics.description: Add the OpenAI action to a Zap to summarise incoming emails, classify form responses, or draft replies automatically.

steps.d: In an existing Zap or new one, add the OpenAI action step and authenticate with your OpenAI API key.
Configure the OpenAI action to take an incoming email body and run a prompt like 'Summarise this email in one bullet point.'
Take the OpenAI response (the summary) and map it to a downstream action like adding a label on the email or sending to Slack.
Send yourself a test email and verify the OpenAI action summarises it correctly and the summary appears in the downstream action.
Modify the prompt to classify incoming emails into 'Urgent', 'Follow-up', or 'FYI' and route each to a different folder.

topics.title: Claude and AI in Make Scenarios
topics.description: Use the HTTP module in Make to call the Anthropic API, pass dynamic text, and route outputs to downstream modules.

steps.d: Sign up for the Anthropic console, create an API key, and copy it to a secure location.
Create a new Make scenario and add an HTTP module as the second step after a trigger.
In the HTTP module, set up a POST request to https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages with your API key and request body.
Connect the trigger data to the HTTP request body so incoming text (e.g. from email or form) is passed to Claude as the user prompt.
Take Claude's response and pass it to a downstream module such as Slack or a database, then test the workflow.

topics.title: AI-Powered Data Processing
topics.description: Build automations that extract structured fields from documents, enrich records with AI-generated tags, and write results to a database.

steps.d: Create a Zap that watches for files in a folder, passes the content to OpenAI with an extraction prompt (e.g. 'Extract name, email, phone'), and saves results to a spreadsheet.
Modify your AI prompt to end with 'Return only valid JSON in the format {name: ..., email: ..., phone: ...}' so the output is machine-readable.
Insert a step after the AI action to parse the JSON response so each field (name, email, phone) can be mapped individually.
Upload 5-10 real invoices or documents and verify extraction and JSON parsing work correctly for all of them.
Modify the workflow to send extracted data to AI with a second prompt (e.g. 'Suggest a product category'), then append the AI-generated tag to the database.

topics.title: Slack and Gmail Integrations
topics.description: Wire Slack messages and Gmail events into your automations — post notifications, triage emails, and log activity to shared channels.

steps.d: Create a new Zap with a Slack trigger (e.g. 'New message in channel') and select the channel to monitor.
Map the Slack message text, user, and timestamp to fields you'll use in downstream actions.
Add a Gmail action to send an email that includes the Slack message content, and test that the email arrives with Slack data populated.
Create a second Zap that takes certain emails and posts a message in a Slack channel with the email summary.
Add a Google Sheets action that records every Slack message and email exchange in a log sheet for audit and search.

topics.title: Notion and Airtable Automations
topics.description: Create and update Notion pages and Airtable records automatically when upstream events occur, keeping your knowledge base always current.

steps.d: Set up a Zap with a trigger (e.g. new email, form submission) and an action that creates a new Notion database page with the trigger data.
Map incoming fields to Notion page properties (e.g. sender → Author, email date → Date, subject → Title) so the database stays populated.
Create a Zap where a Slack emoji reaction triggers an Airtable record update (e.g. click a checkmark emoji to mark the task 'Done').
Build a workflow that reads new rows from Airtable and creates matching records in Notion so both databases stay in sync.
Create a trigger event (e.g. send an email, post to Slack, add an Airtable row) and trace the data through Notion to confirm bidirectional sync.

topics.title: Google Sheets Automation
topics.description: Append rows, update cells, and trigger automations from Sheets events using Zapier and Make.com integrations.

steps.d: Set up a Zap where each trigger event (e.g. new email, form submission) appends a row to a Google Sheet with relevant fields.
Create a second Zap that reads data from the same sheet (using 'Find row' or 'Find all rows') to power a downstream action.
Set up a Zap to watch for new rows in Google Sheets (e.g. when status changes to 'Ready') and trigger an action (e.g. send notification).
Build a workflow that reads text from a Sheets cell, sends it to an AI model, and writes the AI response back to an adjacent cell.
Create a summary sheet that tracks how many times your automations ran, what errors occurred, and how many rows were processed.

topics.title: Planning an End-to-End Automation
topics.description: Map the full trigger-to-outcome flow for a real business process, identify edge cases, and spec out the required steps before building.

steps.d: Draw all steps for a real automation you want to build: trigger → filters → actions → error cases → final output.
Identify every piece of data that needs to flow through your workflow and note any transformations (e.g. format dates, concatenate names).
Ask: 'What if the email has no attachment? What if the amount is zero? What if the user is not in the database?' and add handling steps.
Write a one-page spec: trigger, success criteria, data fields, error handling, and expected weekly volume.
Share your spec with a colleague or manager and confirm they agree the automation solves a real problem and edge cases are covered.

topics.title: Testing and Debugging Workflows
topics.description: Use test runs, step-by-step execution history, and mock data to find and fix failures in your automation before going live.

steps.d: In Zapier or Make, use test mode to send sample data through your workflow without executing real actions.
Step through your workflow one node at a time, verifying that data transforms correctly at each stage and outputs match expectations.
Turn on your Zap or scenario and monitor the execution log for the first 10-20 runs to spot any patterns of failure.
Insert additional steps or log messages that capture intermediate values so you can see exactly where a failure occurs.
Deliberately send malformed, empty, or unusual data through your workflow to ensure it handles errors gracefully.

topics.title: Monitoring and Maintenance
topics.description: Set up error alerts, review task usage, handle API-change breakages, and keep your automations running reliably over time.

steps.d: In your Zapier or Make account, configure notifications via email or Slack to alert you when workflows fail or usage limits are reached.
Check your dashboard weekly to see how many tasks your automations consumed and verify you're on track for your billing tier.
Once per week, open the 'Failed tasks' or 'Incomplete executions' section and read 2-3 failures to spot patterns.
When an integrated app releases API updates, test your workflow and update field mappings if app schemas change.
Write a one-page playbook: what to check weekly, how to fix common failures, and when to rebuild a step because an app deprecated a feature.
